I frequently look behind me to check if someone is following me

issues.item: Threat: Risky Behavior: Taking too many risks or doing things that could cause you harm
issues.explanation: 'Risky Behavior' is hard to reconcile with the rest of the profile, which is dominated by high threat perception, safety behaviors, severe hopelessness, and a robbery-related fear structure. A patient who is persistently choosing safe seats and feeling intensely endangered would more plausibly show avoidance/hypervigilance than generalized risk-taking; this reads as an opposing clinical state within the Threat node.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Authority Figures: Being around people in authority or uniform
issues.explanation: 'Avoid Authority Figures' is a weak fit for mugging/robbery trauma in this profile. There is no supporting trigger, memory, or appraisal content involving police, security staff, uniforms, or institutional betrayal, so this strategy targets a symptom context not otherwise represented in the formulation. For this trauma type, avoiding authority/uniformed people is not impossible, but here it lacks clinical linkage and appears incoherent with the rest of the selected items.

vignette:
At 44, Somchai had built a life that seemed orderly from the outside: he worked long shifts as a nurse, came home to his wife, and tried to keep up the steady routines that had always made him feel useful and in control. That order cracked on an evening walk after a late shift, when two men stepped out near the car park outside a corner shop, one of them blocking his path while the other yanked at his bag and shoved him hard against the wall. Somchai remembered the smell of exhaust, the harsh fluorescent light, and the shock of his shoulder and ribs striking the bricks; afterward, what stayed with him was not a full story but a sequence of vivid pictures, almost like photographs, each frame fixed and bright in his mind. He could see the angle of the men's faces, the hand on his jacket, the pavement under his shoes, and when the memory came back it brought a sharp, bodily ache in the same places that had been bruised that night. From the beginning he was left with the sense that there was something about him that had made it happen, that nothing good could happen to him anymore, and that he had no future that felt secure.

Those beliefs settled quickly into the way Somchai moved through the world. He started arranging his day around what felt safest, choosing where to sit in restaurants, in staff rooms, and even on the bus based on which seat gave him the best view of the door or the most protection from being approached. At work on the ward he kept his mind occupied all the time so he would not drift back to the mugging, but the effort of constant distraction made him tired and irritable. He checked mirrors repeatedly, and as he left the hospital at night he scanned doorways, parked cars, and the edges of the car park, still expecting danger to be waiting just out of sight. Because he believed something in him had drawn the attack, he became more watchful in a way that made the world seem even less forgiving; every shadow confirmed the feeling that he was vulnerable and that his future had already narrowed.

The more he tried to protect himself, the more the event seemed to stay alive in his mind. His scanning of the ward corridors and parking areas, and his habit of looking behind him whenever he heard footsteps, kept the robbery in a constant state of near-presence, so that ordinary moments began to cue the same images of the wall, the hands, and the force of the shove. At night he slept badly, waking again and again, and each broken stretch of sleep left the pictures of the assault closer to the surface. In the mornings he would replay the night in fragments, and the more he searched for signs of threat, the more the memory returned in those sharp visual flashes, accompanied by the same physical pain in his shoulder and ribs. Somchai came to read these intrusions as proof that he was damaged and that his life had already been reduced to waiting for the next attack.

His self-blame deepened alongside those symptoms. Because he was constantly checking his surroundings and choosing protected seats, he felt confirmed in the belief that he was not the sort of man who could simply relax or trust that he would be safe; the very effort of staying safe seemed to tell him he had failed in some basic way. When the images returned at work, he would become more tense and vigilant, and afterward he would judge himself for being unable to put the event behind him. That judgement fed the thought that there was something intrinsic in him that had brought this on, and with it the conviction that nothing good could happen to him anymore. Even at home, his wife noticed that he sat with his back to the wall and glanced into mirrors as he passed, as if the world might catch him unprepared from behind.

By the time he sought help, Somchai was exhausted by the cycle of being on guard, sleeping poorly, and feeling that the mugging still defined what his life could become. He had not told many people how often he looked behind him, how carefully he chose seats, or how much effort it took to keep his mind busy during a shift, but these habits had narrowed his days and strained his sense of himself as a capable husband and nurse. What brought him in was the fear that he would never feel safe again, and the dawning dread that his children and wife were beginning to see him as permanently changed. He hoped, with some uncertainty, that treatment might help him stop living as though the attack were still happening, but he was most afraid that the future he had imagined had already been taken from him.
